title: Troubadours
objective: After this level you can describe the traveling poet-musicians of medieval Europe.
summary: Troubadours, Occitan poet-musicians of the late 11th to late 13th century, were favored at courts. About 2,600 poems survive, fewer than 300 melodies; one trobairitz song keeps its tune.

cards.headline: The first troubadour we know of was a duke.
cards.body: William IX, duke of Aquitaine, born in 1071, wrote songs in Occitan, the language of southern France. His are the earliest troubadour poems to survive. Over the next two centuries, a whole culture of poet-musicians grew up around songs like his. Who were they, and where did most of their tunes go?

cards.headline: The finders of songs
cards.body: Troubadour comes from the Occitan trobar, 'to find' or 'to invent': a troubadour found new songs. From the late 11th to the late 13th century they wrote words and music across southern France, northern Spain and northern Italy. Favored at noble courts, they wrapped the ladies of the court in poems of love. The idea traveled north and east: trouvères in northern France and Minnesingers in Germany wrote their own words and music too.

cards.fact: About 2,600 troubadour poems survive. Fewer than 300 melodies do.
cards.context: The songs, by some 450 troubadours, were copied into songbooks called chansonniers, but most were saved without their tunes. So for the great majority, we can read the poem and only guess how it sounded. Remember Level 25: a melody that isn't written down lasts only as long as someone remembers it.

cards.headline: The women troubadours
cards.body: Women composed too; they're called trobairitz. The Comtessa de Dia, probably named Beatriz, was active around 1175. Her song A chantar is the only trobairitz song that survives with its music. One tune stands in for a whole lost chorus of women's voices.

mascot.line: One surviving melody. Worth a listen if you find a recording.
